title: Esther 8:9–17
context: Mordecai dictates the counter-decree, sent in every language to all 127 provinces. It allows the Jews to gather and defend their lives on the very day Haman had set for their destruction. The wording of 8:11 mirrors Haman’s decree in 3:13, including the mention of little ones, women, and plunder; readers differ on whether “their little ones and women” refers to the families of the attackers or to the Jews’ own families under assault, and the text does not settle it. Mordecai goes out in royal clothing, the city of Susa rejoices, and Jews in every province celebrate, while many from the peoples of the land become Jews, “for the fear of the Jews had fallen on them” (8:17). The book still does not name God; the reversal of mourning (4:3) into gladness is often read as hidden providence, and both traditions treat that as shared ground without decoding every detail.

verses.text: Then the king’s scribes were called at that time, in the third month, which is the month Sivan, on the twenty-third day of the month; and it was written according to all that Mordecai commanded to the Jews, and to the local governors, and the governors and princes of the provinces which are from India to Ethiopia, one hundred twenty-seven provinces, to every province according to its writing, and to every people in their language, and to the Jews in their writing, and in their language.
verses.arminianNotes: The scribes write on the twenty-third of Sivan, according to all Mordecai commanded, to every province and people in their own language, and to the Jews in theirs. Arminian readers note the thoroughness of the effort to reach everyone in time.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the parallel with Haman’s decree (3:12) and the careful reversal of its machinery. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the story’s mirroring of Haman’s plot, with the same channels now used for protection.

verses.text: He wrote in the name of King Ahasuerus, and sealed it with the king’s ring, and sent letters by courier on horseback, riding on royal horses that were bred from swift steeds.
verses.arminianNotes: Mordecai writes in the king’s name, seals it with the king’s ring, and sends couriers on royal horses. Arminian readers note the urgency of the work. The speed of the couriers reflects the need to give the Jews time to prepare before the appointed day.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the urgency and the use of royal authority to counter Haman’s decree. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as historical narrative of the decree’s dispatch, with no doctrinal question raised by the details.

verses.text: In those letters, the king granted the Jews who were in every city to gather themselves together and to defend their lives—to destroy, to kill, and to cause to perish all the power of the people and province that would assault them, their little ones and women, and to plunder their possessions,
verses.arminianNotes: The letters allow the Jews to gather and defend their lives against any force that would attack them. Arminian readers note that the language mirrors Haman’s decree (3:13), and that the text does not settle whose little ones and women are meant. They read the verse soberly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the decree as permission for self-defense against those who would assault the Jews, and they note the same unresolved wording. Shared ground: both traditions describe the decree plainly, without endorsing or excusing every phrase, and without turning it into a modern political argument.

verses.text: on one day in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is the month Adar.
verses.arminianNotes: The counter-decree applies on one day in all the provinces, the thirteenth of Adar. Arminian readers note that this is the very day Haman’s decree had set for the Jews’ destruction (3:13). The danger and the means of defense now meet on the same date.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the deliberate correspondence of dates. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the story’s pattern of reversal, in which the day chosen by lot for destruction becomes a day of deliverance.

verses.text: A copy of the letter, that the decree should be given out in every province, was published to all the peoples, that the Jews should be ready for that day to avenge themselves on their enemies.
verses.arminianNotes: A copy of the decree is published to all peoples so that the Jews can be ready to avenge themselves on their enemies. Arminian readers note the public nature of the decree, which warns potential attackers and prepares the Jews. The verse records the decree’s purpose as given.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the verse as describing the decree’s publication and aim, without expanding on it. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly as part of the narrative and see the readiness of the Jews as a response to the threat of Haman’s decree.

verses.text: So the couriers who rode on royal horses went out, hastened and pressed on by the king’s commandment. The decree was given out in the citadel of Susa.
verses.arminianNotes: The couriers ride out in haste at the king’s command, and the decree is given out in Susa. Arminian readers note the urgency of spreading the word. Time matters, and the king’s officials act quickly to give the Jews a fair opportunity to defend themselves.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the parallel with 3:15, where Haman’s decree was sent out in haste. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the mirroring of the two decrees, and neither finds a doctrinal question in the couriers’ speed.

verses.text: Mordecai went out of the presence of the king in royal clothing of blue and white, and with a great crown of gold, and with a robe of fine linen and purple; and the city of Susa shouted and was glad.
verses.arminianNotes: Mordecai goes out in royal clothing of blue and white, with a great golden crown and a robe of fine linen and purple, and Susa shouts for joy. Arminian readers note the contrast with his sackcloth in 4:1. Mourning has been turned to honor.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the reversal from sackcloth to royal robes and, with many readers, discern God’s hidden hand, though the book does not name him. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a joyful turning point and avoid decoding the colors or garments.

verses.text: The Jews had light, gladness, joy, and honor.
verses.arminianNotes: “The Jews had light, gladness, joy, and honor.” Arminian readers note the piling up of words for joy after a season of fear. The verse captures the relief of a people who were facing death and now have hope.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the joy of deliverance, which the book records without naming God. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a celebration of rescue, and both see in it the fitting response of a people who have been brought from mourning to gladness.

verses.text: In every province and in every city, wherever the king’s commandment and his decree came, the Jews had gladness, joy, a feast and a holiday. Many from among the peoples of the land became Jews, for the fear of the Jews had fallen on them.
verses.arminianNotes: Jews in every province celebrate with feasting, and many from the peoples of the land become Jews, for the fear of the Jews has fallen on them. Arminian readers note that people choose to identify with the Jews, though the text gives fear as the reason.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the conversions and their stated motive, without overreading them. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as describing a dramatic reversal of public sentiment, and both take the narrator’s explanation as given rather than speculating about inner faith.
